ai-at-work.title: Grand Theft Auto VI proves why efficiency isn’t a virtue
ai-at-work.excerpt: On the same day that Anthropic entered the public market, a painstakingly human video game became one of most successful entertainment launches of all time.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Rockstar Games' GTA VI launched as a cultural juggernaut while Anthropic went public, with the game succeeding precisely because humans took years crafting intricate details rather than rushing to market with AI efficiency. This matters to digital workplace folks because it's a reminder that some things genuinely require the messy, time-consuming work of actual human creativity and judgment, not just faster automation. We've spent so long optimizing for speed that we forgot the best experiences often come from people who refused to cut corners, which is maybe the most punk rock thing about a game involving grand theft and chaos.

ai-at-work.title: SAP reportedly plans to lay off 10,000+ employees amid AI push
ai-at-work.excerpt: Enterprise software giant SAP SE is reportedly planning to lay off at least 10,000 employees, or more than 9% of its workforce. Bloomberg today cited sources as saying that the scope of the restructur
ai-at-work.dwp_take: SAP is cutting over 10,000 jobs (9% of staff) while simultaneously pivoting hard into AI development. This matters because SAP is a cornerstone platform for enterprise workflows everywhere, so leadership upheaval and shifting R&D priorities will ripple through countless organizations relying on their tools. Here's the irony: they're laying off people to fund AI that'll supposedly make workers more productive, which is like burning down your house to test a new thermostat.

ai-at-work.title: Wireless networking chip startup Altair nabs $100M investment
ai-at-work.excerpt: Altair Semiconductor Ltd., a supplier of wireless networking chips for connected devices, today announced that it has raised $100 million in funding. Maverick Silicon led the Series A round. It was re
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Altair Semiconductor just raised $100 million to build wireless chips for connected devices, with Maverick Silicon leading the round and Pitango doubling down on its earlier investment after the company spun out of Sony. This matters because workplace devices need reliable connectivity, and new chip tech directly impacts whether your video calls drop and your collaboration tools actually respond when you need them. Here's the thing though: another wireless chip company getting funded is great, but what really counts is whether these chips actually make our networks less temperamental than they currently are, and I'll believe that when I see it working consistently across a Monday morning.

Here's my take:

The article explains that traditional security models built on "who can do what" fall apart with AI agents because authorization alone doesn't prevent damage when those agents operate at scale and speed humans can't monitor. This matters because most organizations are deploying AI tools into their workflows right now while still using 20-year-old permission frameworks that treat a human clicking a button the same as an AI making a thousand decisions per second. tools-tech.excerpt: OpenAI has corrected a billing error that undercounted usage of its GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol models, warning customers that the same workloads will now consume more of their subscription allowances and c
tools-tech.dwp_take: OpenAI quietly corrected a billing glitch on GPT-6.2 that means your tokens now cost more, with some workloads burning through your monthly allowance 40% faster than you thought they were. This matters because workplace AI spend is suddenly becoming a lot less predictable, and those budget forecasts your CFO signed off on just got messier. Nothing says "trust us with your enterprise data" like finding out you're getting less bang for your buck without asking permission first.

digital-culture.title: Screen time got your brain fried? Try a ‘brain stack’
digital-culture.excerpt: Every few months, like clockwork, a new analog trend emerges in an effort to get us all off our phones. . .and of course, document the process for social media. The latest is “brain stacking”: keeping
digital-culture.dwp_take: Some folks are literally stacking analog activities next to their desks as a physical barrier against phone addiction. This matters because if your workforce is constantly context-switching between Slack, email, and TikTok, productivity tanks and nobody's actually thinking deeply anymore. Look, I'm all for reducing screen time, but let's be honest: the real problem isn't the stack of books collecting dust, it's that your company culture rewards hyperresponsiveness over actual work.

digital-culture.title: Workers hoard AI knowledge to stay competitive, Anthropic report says
digital-culture.excerpt: AI tools are becoming increasingly ubiquitous, but the best techniques for using them are likely still a secret. This is because workers who develop highly effective AI tricks have no incentive to sha
digital-culture.dwp_take: Workers are keeping their best AI techniques to themselves instead of sharing them with colleagues because they see it as job security. This matters because it creates knowledge silos that tank productivity and make organizations waste money buying AI tools they can't actually use well. Here's the thing: if your workplace culture is so cutthroat that people hide what they know, you've already lost the game, because AI's real value comes from teams that share and iterate together.

digital-culture.title: 6 tips to use this Thanksgiving when family asks about your career
digital-culture.excerpt: Evan Reece has a few strategies for handling unwelcome questions about his career when he gathers with family. He founded and ran a ski lift ticket platform for 15 years, but it went out of business d
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company published career advice for handling awkward family questions about work, using an entrepreneur who lost his ski ticket business in the pandemic and now runs a solo career platform that pays less than his old gig. This matters because digital workplace professionals deal with constant career pivots, layoffs, and income shifts these days, and having a framework for talking about it without defensiveness helps. Here's the thing though: if you need tips to explain your job to your relatives, maybe the real issue is that the work itself isn't giving you the confidence to do it naturally.

digital-culture.title: Meta Refused to Share Muse for Testing, UK Financial Watchdog Complains
digital-culture.excerpt: The FCA warned against “another force of attack” from agents after the company declined a request to work on joint testing ahead of rolling out its personal agent in the UK on Tuesday.
digital-culture.dwp_take: Meta declined to let the UK's Financial Conduct Authority test its new Muse AI agent before launch, which prompted the regulator to complain about being shut out of the process. This matters because digital workplace tools handling financial information need independent security vetting, and when vendors skip that step, it creates real compliance headaches for enterprises in regulated industries. After thirty years watching tech companies move fast and break things, I'd say Meta's move is either arrogant or desperate, and neither one builds the trust you need when you're asking people to let AI handle their money.

The real question is whether one model that does everything actually does anything well, or if we're just swapping specialized problems for one giant generalized headache.

industry-news.excerpt: New York’s five-year ban on toys with AI companions starts Feb. 22, 2027. See which toys are covered and what the law means for retailers and toy makers. The post New York’s AI Chatbot Toy Ban: Which
industry-news.dwp_take: New York is banning AI companion toys starting February 2027, which will restrict certain products from being sold in the state for five years. For digital workplace professionals, this signals that regulatory scrutiny around AI is intensifying and companies need to start auditing their AI implementations now rather than waiting for federal guidance. Here's the kicker: if toy makers are getting slapped with restrictions, your enterprise AI tools are definitely in regulators' sights too, so maybe don't wait until 2027 to have that governance conversation.

industry-news.excerpt: Fake Roblox cheat downloads can steal passwords and browser sessions. Here’s what Windows users and IT teams should do if someone runs a fake installer. The post Fake Roblox Cheats Can Steal Passwords
industry-news.dwp_take: Fake Roblox cheat downloads are tricking users into installing malware that harvests passwords and hijacks browser sessions. Here's the real kicker: IT teams spend all year locking down the front door while users are gleefully opening the back door themselves because they want unlimited Robux.

industry-news.title: Anthropic Launches Claude Ship to Review, Fix and Approve GitHub Pull Requests
industry-news.excerpt: Anthropic's Claude Ship brings AI-powered reviews, fixes, and approvals to GitHub pull requests. Here's how its three agents work, what they cost, and where human reviewers remain essential. The post
industry-news.dwp_take: Anthropic released Claude Ship, an AI tool that automates GitHub pull request reviews, fixes code issues, and approves changes using three different agents. This matters to digital workplace teams because it could speed up development cycles and reduce bottlenecks caused by human code review delays. That said, anyone who thinks this replaces actual engineers hasn't spent much time in the real world where context, business logic, and architectural decisions matter way more than syntax checking.
